nameStory: The name "chicken lips" comes from this mushroom's bizarre resemblance to tiny, plump lips when viewed from the side. The green, rubbery cap sits atop a yellow stem like a peculiar mouth, creating one of the most whimsical names in the fungal kingdom. It's also called "jelly baby" for its soft, gelatinous texture that feels like gummy candy.
description: Chicken lips is a small, unusual mushroom that looks more like a tiny alien than a typical toadstool. Instead of the classic cap-and-stem design, it has a distinctive green, blob-like top that sits on a bright yellow stalk. The green "cap" comes in various irregular shapes - sometimes round, sometimes lobed or wrinkled, giving each specimen its own quirky personality. These little fungi typically reach just a few inches tall and have a distinctly rubbery, jelly-like texture.

idTips.label: Color combination
idTips.description: Bright yellow stem topped with a green, jelly-like cap - this striking two-tone color scheme is unmistakable

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: The entire mushroom feels rubbery and gelatinous, like a firm gummy bear - squeeze it gently and it springs back

idTips.label: Cap shape
idTips.description: The green top comes in wildly variable shapes - sometimes round like a button, other times lobed or wrinkled like brain coral

idTips.label: Growing pattern
idTips.description: Often found in small scattered groups rather than large clusters, each mushroom standing like a tiny green-capped sentinel

idTips.label: Surface appearance
idTips.description: The green cap has a smooth, slightly glossy surface that may look wet or sticky even when dry

habitat: Look for chicken lips in deciduous and mixed forests, especially under oak trees where they seem to have a special affinity for the acidic soil. They also pop up on rotting logs and stumps, particularly in areas with rich, moist leaf litter. These little fungi prefer shaded, humid spots in woodlands throughout New England's lower elevations.

seasonality.spring: Generally not visible yet, though warm, wet springs might bring out very early specimens in protected spots.
seasonality.summer: Prime season begins in mid to late summer when humidity is high and temperatures are warm but not scorching.
seasonality.fall: Peak season continues through early fall, with the most abundant fruiting occurring during September's warm, moist weather.
seasonality.winter: Disappears completely once freezing weather arrives, leaving no trace until the following year.

funFact: Despite their bizarre alien appearance, chicken lips mushrooms are part of a group that's more closely related to cup fungi than to typical mushrooms - they're essentially cup fungi that forgot how to make cups and decided to make weird rubbery blobs instead!
confusionNotes: The bright yellow stem with green gelatinous top makes chicken lips nearly impossible to confuse with anything else in New England. The closest confusion might be with other jelly fungi, but none have this specific yellow-and-green color combination.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name "Leotia" honors French botanist Daniel Lecoq, but many field guides list this species under different names due to ongoing taxonomic confusion. Don't be surprised if you see it called "green jelly drops" or simply "jelly baby" in older mushroom books.
compareHints: Chicken lips can be distinguished from its close relative, the ochre jelly club, by its green cap (versus ochre/brownish) and more irregular cap shape. While ochre jelly club tends to have a more club-like or spoon-shaped top, chicken lips displays much more variety in its green cap form. Both share that distinctive rubbery texture and preference for growing near oaks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Ochre Jelly Club differs from Chicken Lips mainly in color - it's more golden-orange while Chicken Lips tends toward yellow-green.
